JMAP_PLACES: The head shrine of Inari, the kami of rice and good fortune. Around 10,000 vermilion torii gates climb Mount Inari in long tunnels.
Foxes (kitsune) are Inari's messengers, so fox statues guard the shrine, often with a key or a jewel in their mouths.
Home! Every journey of mine starts here~
Japan's first permanent capital, from 710. Over a thousand wild sika deer roam Nara Park, and Tōdai-ji houses a bronze Great Buddha about 15 m tall.
The deer are seen as messengers of the gods, and many bow back if you bow to them.
They bow if you bow! Very polite... until you have crackers.
Japan's most sacred Shinto shrine, dedicated to the sun goddess Amaterasu.
The shrine buildings are rebuilt from fresh cypress every 20 years (Shikinen Sengū), a custom kept for about 1,300 years.
Rebuilt every 20 years... like my revision notes.
The capital since 1868 and one of the largest cities on Earth. Sensō-ji in Asakusa, founded in 645, is its oldest temple.
Its old name was Edo. It became Tokyo, 'eastern capital', when the emperor moved there from Kyoto.
So many lights! I'm keeping my tails close.
Japan's highest mountain at 3,776 m: an active volcano that last erupted in 1707, and a sacred mountain for centuries.
The climbing season is roughly July to early September. Watching sunrise from the top is called goraikō.
Ancient pilgrimage trails through the forests of the Kii Peninsula, linking three grand shrines.
It's one of only two pilgrimage routes on the UNESCO World Heritage list; the other is the Camino de Santiago.
The three-legged crow Yatagarasu shows the way. I just follow the crow.
One of Japan's most famous hot springs. Very hot, acidic water steams through the yubatake, the 'hot water field', in the middle of town.
To cool the water without adding any, people stir it with long wooden paddles while singing. It's called yumomi.
Onsen after a long study day... this is the dream.
Tōshō-gū, the richly carved shrine and mausoleum of shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu, among tall cedar forests.
The famous 'see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil' monkeys are carved on its sacred stable.
See no distractions, hear no distractions~
An old castle town with Kenroku-en, one of Japan's three great gardens, plus preserved samurai and geisha districts.
Almost all of Japan's gold leaf (over 99%) is made here.
They put gold leaf on ice cream here. For science, we must try it.
One of Japan's oldest shrines, home of the god Ōkuninushi, who is linked to good relationships and matchmaking.
In the tenth lunar month the gods of Japan are said to gather here, so Izumo calls it Kamiarizuki, 'the month with gods', while everywhere else it's 'the month without gods'.
Every kami in Japan meets up here once a year. Imagine the group chat.
An island shrine whose great vermilion torii seems to float on the sea at high tide.
At low tide you can walk out to the torii. It isn't buried in the seabed; it stands by its own weight.
A torii in the sea! My paws will get wet and I don't care.
A mountain shrine in Shikoku for sailors and seafarers, reached by a long stone stairway.
It's 785 steps to the main hall and 1,368 to the inner shrine.
1,368 steps. That counts as leg day, right?
One of the world's largest volcanic calderas, about 25 km across, with towns and farms inside and an active crater, Nakadake.
The grasslands are kept open by burning them each spring (noyaki), a practice over 1,000 years old.
A whole town inside a volcano. Brave people.
A rainy, moss-covered island of ancient cedar forests, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1993.
Its most famous cedar, Jōmon Sugi, is thought to be at least 2,000 years old, and maybe far older.
Older than every textbook put together. Very calm trees.
'Mount Dread': a volcanic caldera with sulphur vents and a still blue lake, said in folklore to be a gateway to the afterlife.
During its summer festival, mediums called itako are said to pass on messages from spirits.
Spooky but beautiful. Hold my tail, okay?
Hokkaido's capital, famous for its Snow Festival, when giant snow and ice sculptures fill Ōdōri Park each February.
The festival began in 1950, when local high school students built six snow statues.
Snow! I'm very fluffy for exactly this reason.
A wild peninsula at Japan's north-east tip, with brown bears, waterfalls into the sea and drift ice in winter.
Its name comes from the Ainu word for 'the end of the earth'.
The end of the earth... and I walked here with you.
Seat of the Ryūkyū Kingdom, an island kingdom with its own language and culture, for about 450 years.
Its main hall burned down in 2019 and is being rebuilt by traditional methods.
Warm sea, red roofs, shīsā lion-dogs on every gate. We made it!
JOURNEY_REGIONS: Zenko's home: shrines, mountains and islands
One city through spring, summer, autumn and winter
Palaces, temples and a volcano island
Palaces, sacred mountains and karst rivers
Oasis cities from Xi'an to Bukhara

Green hills on Kyoto's west side, with the famous bamboo grove and the Togetsukyō bridge over the river.
Togetsukyō means 'Moon Crossing Bridge': an emperor in the 1200s said the moon looked like it was walking across it.
The bamboo whispers. I think it's saying 'study, study'~
A great Zen temple founded in 1236. In November, the Tsūten-kyō bridge crosses a valley that turns red and gold with about 2,000 maple trees.
Its gate, the Sanmon, is the oldest Zen main gate in Japan.
Momiji season! My fur matches the leaves, ehehe~
The Golden Pavilion: the retirement villa of shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, turned into a Zen temple. Its top two floors are covered in gold leaf.
It burned down in 1950 and was rebuilt in 1955. Seeing it under snow is rare, and very lucky.
Gold and snow... it's like a winter dream~
Kyoto's old geisha district, where geiko and maiko still walk the stone lanes between wooden teahouses.
The Gion Matsuri in July began in 869, as a prayer to end an epidemic. It's one of Japan's biggest festivals.
Lanterns, wooden lanes, the sound of geta... so pretty at dusk.
The main royal palace of the Joseon dynasty, built in 1395. Its name means 'palace greatly blessed by heaven'.
It was burned in the war of 1592 and rebuilt in 1867. You can still watch the colourful changing of the guard.
Royal guards in red and blue! I'm standing very straight now.
A temple of the Silla kingdom, finished in 774, with two famous stone pagodas, Dabotap and Seokgatap.
With the Seokguram grotto on the hill above, it became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1995.
Stone pagodas older than a thousand years. Very patient stones~
A mountain temple that keeps the Tripitaka Koreana: over 81,000 wooden printing blocks of Buddhist scripture, carved in the 1200s.
The halls that store them are built so air flows through naturally, which has kept the wood safe for centuries.
81,000 blocks with no mistakes... the best revision notes ever.
South Korea's highest mountain (1,947 m): a volcano that makes up most of Jeju Island, with a crater lake on top.
Jeju's haenyeo, women who free-dive for seafood without air tanks, are on UNESCO's list of living heritage.
A whole island made by one volcano. The sea breeze is so nice!
One of Korea's few temples by the sea, first built in 1376 on rocks where the waves crash right below.
Its name means 'Dragon Palace Temple', for the Dragon King of the sea.
A temple on the waves. I hope the Dragon King says hello~
The imperial palace of the Ming and Qing dynasties from 1420 to 1912: home to 24 emperors.
Legend says it has 9,999 rooms, one fewer than the 10,000 of the palace of heaven.
So many golden roofs! I'll need a map just for the palace.
Not one wall but many, built and rebuilt over about 2,000 years. The stone sections near Beijing are from the Ming dynasty.
A popular myth says you can see it from the Moon with your eyes. You can't; it's long, but far too narrow.
My paws are tired... but the view from the watchtower is worth it.
The most honoured of China's sacred mountains. For over 2,000 years emperors climbed it to offer sacrifices to heaven.
Pilgrims climb over 6,000 stone steps to the summit to watch the sunrise.
6,000 steps. Leg day again. Exercise tab, are you watching?
A lake of willows, pagodas and causeways that inspired poets and painters for over a thousand years.
The Su Causeway is named after the poet Su Dongpo, who had it built in the 1000s from mud dredged from the lake.
A poet built a whole causeway. I just want to write one good essay~
A temple founded in 495, famous for kung fu and, by tradition, as the cradle of Chan Buddhism, which became Zen in Japan.
The monks' training mixes martial arts with meditation: focus of the body and the mind together.
Zen started here? Then our focus sessions are a little bit Shaolin~
The Yellow Mountains: granite peaks, twisted pines and a 'sea of clouds' that inspired centuries of ink painting.
It has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1990, both for its nature and its culture.
Mountains floating in clouds, like a painting come alive.
Carved into a cliff from 713 to 803, it's 71 m tall: the largest stone Buddha in the world.
A monk started it hoping to calm the dangerous waters where three rivers meet below its feet.
His toenail is bigger than me. I checked.
Hundreds of steep green karst peaks rising along a calm river, a classic view of southern China.
The Li River scenery is printed on the back of China's 20-yuan note.
Mountains like sleeping dragons. Shh, don't wake them~
As Chang'an it was the capital of many dynasties and the eastern start of the Silk Road. Nearby stands the Terracotta Army of the first emperor, Qin Shi Huang.
The terracotta warriors were found in 1974 by farmers digging a well. Each of the thousands of soldiers has its own face.
Thousands of clay soldiers... and not one of them is studying. Hmph.
The fortress at the western end of the Ming Great Wall, built in 1372, where the green lands meet the desert.
Legend says its builders planned the bricks so exactly that only one was left over. It still sits on a gate.
One spare brick. Now that's planning! Like your study planner~
The Mogao Caves: hundreds of cave temples filled with Buddhist paintings made over a thousand years, beside dunes and the Crescent Lake.
A hidden library cave found in 1900 held the Diamond Sutra of 868, the oldest dated printed book in the world.
The sand dunes sing when the wind blows. Really!
An oasis in one of the hottest and lowest places in China, kept green by karez: hand-dug underground water channels.
Nearby are the Flaming Mountains, which a famous story says the Monkey King had to cross in Journey to the West.
So hot! My tails are fanning me as fast as they can.
An ancient oasis city at the western edge of the Taklamakan Desert, where the Silk Road's northern and southern routes met.
Traders crossed the Pamir mountains from here, carrying silk west and bringing glass, horses and spices east.
A market full of spices and melons. I smell everything at once!
One of the oldest cities in Central Asia. Its Registan square is framed by three blue-tiled madrasas from the 1400s to 1600s.
Ulugh Beg built an observatory here in the 1420s and made one of the best star catalogues of his time.
Turquoise domes under the desert sky... and an astronomer who studied the stars!
A holy city of the Silk Road with hundreds of old buildings. The Kalyan Minaret has towered over it since 1127.
A story says Genghis Khan destroyed much of the city in 1220 but spared the minaret because it amazed him.
The end of the road... for now. We walked all the way from Kyoto!
A mountain island of the immortals in Chinese legend, hidden in mist in the eastern sea.
The first emperor sent Xu Fu to find its elixir of life. One legend says he sailed on and settled in Japan.
If I find the elixir, I'll share it with you. Promise.
A paradise mountain in the far west, home of Xiwangmu, the Queen Mother of the West.
Her peaches of immortality ripen only once every 3,000 years, as Journey to the West tells it.
3,000 years for one peach? I'd rather have inari sushi now~
The Dragon King's palace under the sea, from the tale of Urashima Tarō, who saved a turtle and was invited there.
He stayed three days, but 300 years had passed when he got home. The box he was told never to open made him old.
We can visit, but let's not stay too long. Your exams are this year, not in 300 years!
The High Plain of Heaven, where the kami live, in the Kojiki, Japan's oldest chronicle (712).
When the sun goddess Amaterasu hid in a cave, the goddess Ame-no-Uzume danced until everyone laughed, and the light came back out.
When you feel dark, I'll dance for you too. Kon kon~
Guanghan Palace on the Moon, home of Chang'e, who drank the elixir of life and floated up to the sky.
Her friend the Jade Rabbit pounds medicine there. China named its Moon missions Chang'e and its rover Yutu, Jade Rabbit.
We made it to the Moon! The Jade Rabbit says hello~
In fox legends, a kitsune grows a new tail every hundred years. With nine tails and a thousand years, its fur turns gold and it becomes a heavenly fox.
Kitsune are said to make foxfire, kitsunebi, with their tails. That's where my glow comes from!
Here is where every fox dreams of going. And I came here... with you. Arigatou.

westlake: A lake of willows, pagodas and causeways that inspired poets and painters for over a thousand years.
The Su Causeway is named after the poet Su Dongpo, who had it built in the 1000s from mud dredged from the lake.
A poet built a whole causeway. I just want to write one good essay~
shaolin: A temple founded in 495, famous for kung fu and, by tradition, as the cradle of Chan Buddhism, which became Zen in Japan.
The monks' training mixes martial arts with meditation: focus of the body and the mind together.
Zen started here? Then our focus sessions are a little bit Shaolin~
huangshan: The Yellow Mountains: granite peaks, twisted pines and a 'sea of clouds' that inspired centuries of ink painting.
It has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1990, both for its nature and its culture.
Mountains floating in clouds, like a painting come alive.
leshan: Carved into a cliff from 713 to 803, it's 71 m tall: the largest stone Buddha in the world.
A monk started it hoping to calm the dangerous waters where three rivers meet below its feet.
His toenail is bigger than me. I checked.
guilin: Hundreds of steep green karst peaks rising along a calm river, a classic view of southern China.
The Li River scenery is printed on the back of China's 20-yuan note.
Mountains like sleeping dragons. Shh, don't wake them~
xian: As Chang'an it was the capital of many dynasties and the eastern start of the Silk Road. Nearby stands the Terracotta Army of the first emperor, Qin Shi Huang.
The terracotta warriors were found in 1974 by farmers digging a well. Each of the thousands of soldiers has its own face.
Thousands of clay soldiers... and not one of them is studying. Hmph.
jiayuguan: The fortress at the western end of the Ming Great Wall, built in 1372, where the green lands meet the desert.
Legend says its builders planned the bricks so exactly that only one was left over. It still sits on a gate.
One spare brick. Now that's planning! Like your study planner~
dunhuang: The Mogao Caves: hundreds of cave temples filled with Buddhist paintings made over a thousand years, beside dunes and the Crescent Lake.
A hidden library cave found in 1900 held the Diamond Sutra of 868, the oldest dated printed book in the world.
The sand dunes sing when the wind blows. Really!
turpan: An oasis in one of the hottest and lowest places in China, kept green by karez: hand-dug underground water channels.
Nearby are the Flaming Mountains, which a famous story says the Monkey King had to cross in Journey to the West.
So hot! My tails are fanning me as fast as they can.
kashgar: An ancient oasis city at the western edge of the Taklamakan Desert, where the Silk Road's northern and southern routes met.
Traders crossed the Pamir mountains from here, carrying silk west and bringing glass, horses and spices east.
A market full of spices and melons. I smell everything at once!
samarkand: One of the oldest cities in Central Asia. Its Registan square is framed by three blue-tiled madrasas from the 1400s to 1600s.
Ulugh Beg built an observatory here in the 1420s and made one of the best star catalogues of his time.
Turquoise domes under the desert sky... and an astronomer who studied the stars!
bukhara: A holy city of the Silk Road with hundreds of old buildings. The Kalyan Minaret has towered over it since 1127.
A story says Genghis Khan destroyed much of the city in 1220 but spared the minaret because it amazed him.
The end of the road... for now. We walked all the way from Kyoto!
penglai: A mountain island of the immortals in Chinese legend, hidden in mist in the eastern sea.
The first emperor sent Xu Fu to find its elixir of life. One legend says he sailed on and settled in Japan.
If I find the elixir, I'll share it with you. Promise.
kunlun: A paradise mountain in the far west, home of Xiwangmu, the Queen Mother of the West.
Her peaches of immortality ripen only once every 3,000 years, as Journey to the West tells it.
3,000 years for one peach? I'd rather have inari sushi now~
ryugu: The Dragon King's palace under the sea, from the tale of Urashima Tarō, who saved a turtle and was invited there.
He stayed three days, but 300 years had passed when he got home. The box he was told never to open made him old.
We can visit, but let's not stay too long. Your exams are this year, not in 300 years!
takamagahara: The High Plain of Heaven, where the kami live, in the Kojiki, Japan's oldest chronicle (712).
When the sun goddess Amaterasu hid in a cave, the goddess Ame-no-Uzume danced until everyone laughed, and the light came back out.
When you feel dark, I'll dance for you too. Kon kon~
guanghan: Guanghan Palace on the Moon, home of Chang'e, who drank the elixir of life and floated up to the sky.
Her friend the Jade Rabbit pounds medicine there. China named its Moon missions Chang'e and its rover Yutu, Jade Rabbit.
We made it to the Moon! The Jade Rabbit says hello~
kyubi: In fox legends, a kitsune grows a new tail every hundred years. With nine tails and a thousand years, its fur turns gold and it becomes a heavenly fox.
Kitsune are said to make foxfire, kitsunebi, with their tails. That's where my glow comes from!
Here is where every fox dreams of going. And I came here... with you. Arigatou.

JOURNEY_MORE: A hillside temple founded in 778. Its great wooden stage juts out over the trees and was built without a single nail. In spring it floats over a sea of cherry blossom.
'To jump off the stage of Kiyomizu' is a Japanese saying for taking a bold leap, like starting a big project.
Sakura everywhere! Let's take the plunge into Chapter 5~
Green hills on Kyoto's west side, with the famous bamboo grove and the Togetsukyō bridge over the river.
Togetsukyō means 'Moon Crossing Bridge': an emperor in the 1200s said the moon looked like it was walking across it.
The bamboo whispers. I think it's saying 'study, study'~
A great Zen temple founded in 1236. In November, the Tsūten-kyō bridge crosses a valley that turns red and gold with about 2,000 maple trees.
Its gate, the Sanmon, is the oldest Zen main gate in Japan.
Momiji season! My fur matches the leaves, ehehe~
The Golden Pavilion: the retirement villa of shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, turned into a Zen temple. Its top two floors are covered in gold leaf.
It burned down in 1950 and was rebuilt in 1955. Seeing it under snow is rare, and very lucky.
Gold and snow... it's like a winter dream~
Kyoto's old geisha district, where geiko and maiko still walk the stone lanes between wooden teahouses.
The Gion Matsuri in July began in 869, as a prayer to end an epidemic. It's one of Japan's biggest festivals.
Lanterns, wooden lanes, the sound of geta... so pretty at dusk.
The main royal palace of the Joseon dynasty, built in 1395. Its name means 'palace greatly blessed by heaven'.
It was burned in the war of 1592 and rebuilt in 1867. You can still watch the colourful changing of the guard.
Royal guards in red and blue! I'm standing very straight now.
A temple of the Silla kingdom, finished in 774, with two famous stone pagodas, Dabotap and Seokgatap.
With the Seokguram grotto on the hill above, it became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1995.
Stone pagodas older than a thousand years. Very patient stones~
A mountain temple that keeps the Tripitaka Koreana: over 81,000 wooden printing blocks of Buddhist scripture, carved in the 1200s.
The halls that store them are built so air flows through naturally, which has kept the wood safe for centuries.
81,000 blocks with no mistakes... the best revision notes ever.
South Korea's highest mountain (1,947 m): a volcano that makes up most of Jeju Island, with a crater lake on top.
Jeju's haenyeo, women who free-dive for seafood without air tanks, are on UNESCO's list of living heritage.
A whole island made by one volcano. The sea breeze is so nice!
One of Korea's few temples by the sea, first built in 1376 on rocks where the waves crash right below.
Its name means 'Dragon Palace Temple', for the Dragon King of the sea.
A temple on the waves. I hope the Dragon King says hello~
The imperial palace of the Ming and Qing dynasties from 1420 to 1912: home to 24 emperors.
Legend says it has 9,999 rooms, one fewer than the 10,000 of the palace of heaven.
So many golden roofs! I'll need a map just for the palace.
Not one wall but many, built and rebuilt over about 2,000 years. The stone sections near Beijing are from the Ming dynasty.
A popular myth says you can see it from the Moon with your eyes. You can't; it's long, but far too narrow.
My paws are tired... but the view from the watchtower is worth it.
The most honoured of China's sacred mountains. For over 2,000 years emperors climbed it to offer sacrifices to heaven.
Pilgrims climb over 6,000 stone steps to the summit to watch the sunrise.
